stages.title: How Sound Works
stages.description: Sound is a vibration measured in hertz and decibels. Pitch and loudness are what the ear makes of those numbers, and loud sound damages hearing for good.
learningObjectives: Connect frequency in hertz to the pitch a listener hears
Read the decibel scale as a ratio, not a straight line
Separate measured intensity from perceived loudness
State the exposure levels that put hearing at risk

explainBack.question: A friend turns a sound up by 10 dB and says it is now just a little louder. Explain what changed physically, how pitch and loudness relate to the numbers, and when that level starts to put their hearing at risk.
rubric: Frequency is the number of vibrations per second, measured in hertz, and the ear perceives it as pitch
Humans hear roughly 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz, and doubling the frequency raises the pitch by one octave
The decibel scale is logarithmic: each +10 dB is ten times the intensity, and 0 dB is the threshold of hearing
Loudness is a perception; the ear is most sensitive in the middle frequencies, so equal intensity does not sound equally loud
Long or repeated exposure at or above 85 dBA can cause permanent noise-induced hearing loss, because damaged hair cells do not grow back

resources.title: Pitch and Frequency
resources.description: What frequency is, how the ear turns it into pitch, and the range of human hearing.
keyPoints: Frequency is the number of complete vibrations per second, measured in hertz (Hz)
Humans hear frequencies from about 20 Hz to about 20,000 Hz; below is infrasound and above is ultrasound
Pitch is the sensation of a frequency: a high frequency is heard as a high pitch
Two sounds with a 2:1 frequency ratio are an octave apart
Sounds whose frequencies form simple whole-number ratios tend to sound pleasant together

resources.title: Intensity and the Decibel Scale
resources.description: Intensity, the inverse square law, and why the decibel scale counts in powers of ten.
keyPoints: Intensity is the energy a sound carries through an area per second, and it falls with the square of the distance from the source
0 dB is the threshold of hearing, an intensity of 1 x 10^-12 W/m^2
Each increase of 10 dB is a tenfold increase in intensity, so 20 dB is 100 times more intense than 0 dB
Normal conversation is about 60 dB and the threshold of pain is about 130 dB
Perceived loudness is subjective, and the ear is most sensitive to frequencies around 1,000 to 5,000 Hz

resources.title: Noise-Induced Hearing Loss
resources.provider: National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders (NIDCD)
resources.description: Which levels damage hearing, why the damage is permanent, and how to prevent it.
keyPoints: Sounds at or below 70 dBA are unlikely to harm hearing, even after long exposure
Long or repeated exposure to sounds at or above 85 dBA can cause hearing loss
Personal listening devices at maximum volume can reach roughly 94 to 110 dBA
Noise damages the sensory hair cells in the inner ear, and in humans those cells do not grow back
Noise-induced hearing loss is preventable: lower the volume, move away from the source, limit the time, and wear earplugs or earmuffs

stages.title: Digital Audio Basics
stages.description: A recording is a list of samples. Sample rate sets the highest frequency it can hold, bit depth sets the dynamic range, and anything over 0 dB clips.
learningObjectives: Explain what a sample rate is and why it has to be more than twice the highest frequency
Connect bit depth to dynamic range
Recognise clipping and why it happens
Choose between a lossless and a lossy file for a task

explainBack.question: You are setting up a session to record dialogue for a short film. Explain which sample rate and bit depth you would pick, what each number controls, what clipping is, and which file format you would keep as the master.
rubric: Digital audio stores the waveform as samples taken at a fixed sample rate
The sample rate must be more than twice the highest frequency to be captured (the Nyquist rule); otherwise aliasing adds false tones
CD audio uses 44.1 kHz, which covers the roughly 20 kHz limit of human hearing
Bit depth sets dynamic range: 16-bit gives about 96 dB and 24-bit about 145 dB
A signal that goes above 0 dB clips and distorts, so leave headroom
Keep the master lossless (WAV or FLAC); MP3 is lossy and throws away detail using psychoacoustics

resources.title: Digital Audio Fundamentals
resources.description: Samples, sample rates, bit depth, clipping, and file formats explained by the Audacity team.
keyPoints: Digital audio is a sequence of samples; the sample rate is how many are taken each second
To represent a frequency the sample rate must be more than twice that frequency (Nyquist); otherwise the result is aliasing
CD audio is sampled at 44,100 Hz, enough for the upper limit of human hearing
Bit depth (sample format) sets dynamic range: 16-bit is about 96 dB, 24-bit about 145 dB, and 32-bit float is effectively unlimited
Samples above 0 dB are clipped, which causes distortion
MP3 and similar formats are lossy and use psychoacoustics to discard detail; FLAC is lossless; uncompressed size is sample rate x bit depth x channels x seconds

stages.title: Recording & Microphones
stages.description: A microphone's polar pattern decides what it hears and what it rejects. Distance changes the tone. Room tone recorded on set saves the edit later.
learningObjectives: Compare omnidirectional, cardioid, hypercardioid, figure-8, and shotgun patterns
Explain the proximity effect
Aim a microphone's null at an unwanted noise
Record usable room tone on location

explainBack.question: You are recording an interview in a room with a noisy air-conditioner behind the speaker's left shoulder. Explain which microphone pattern you would choose, where you would point it, how close you would place it, and what you would record before you leave the room.
rubric: An omnidirectional mic picks up sound equally from all directions; a directional mic favours the front
A cardioid is quieter at the sides and most rejecting directly behind, so off-axis noise is reduced
Each pattern has nulls, such as 180 degrees for cardioid, and the null should be aimed at the noise
Moving a directional mic very close raises the bass (proximity effect), so distance changes tone as well as level
Shotgun mics are used on film sets because they reject more sound from the sides
Record about 30 to 60 seconds of room tone with the same mic, placement, and settings, so gaps and cuts can be filled later

resources.title: A Brief Guide to Microphones - What's The Pattern?
resources.description: Omnidirectional and directional patterns, how much each rejects, and when to use them.
keyPoints: An omnidirectional mic responds equally to sound from all directions; a directional mic is most sensitive at the front
A cardioid is about 6 dB less sensitive at the sides (90 degrees) and about 20 dB less sensitive at the rear (180 degrees)
A cardioid picks up about one third of the ambient sound an omni does, and can be placed about 1.7 times farther away for the same balance
Directional mics show a proximity effect: bass rises when the source is very close
Line (shotgun) mics are the most directional and suit film, video, and distant pickup
Directional pickup helps reduce feedback from loudspeakers

resources.title: Understanding & Using Directional Microphones
resources.author: Hugh Robjohns
resources.description: Why pressure and pressure-gradient designs behave differently, and how to use the nulls.
keyPoints: Microphones work on two principles: pressure (omnidirectional) and pressure gradient (figure-8)
Combining omni and figure-8 responses gives cardioid, supercardioid, and hypercardioid patterns
Pressure-gradient designs show the proximity effect, a bass boost close to the source
The nulls sit at about 180 degrees for a cardioid, about 130 degrees either side for a hypercardioid, and at 90 degrees for a figure-8
Pointing the null at the unwanted source is often more useful than pointing the front at the wanted one

resources.title: What Is Room Tone in Film?
resources.description: What room tone is, why the edit needs it, and how to record it on set.
keyPoints: Room tone is the natural ambient sound of a location when nobody is speaking
It is used to fill gaps, smooth dialogue cuts, and blend ADR into the scene
Record at least 30 to 60 seconds, with the same microphone, placement, and settings used for the takes
Everyone on set stays still and quiet while it is recorded, usually after the last take
Room tone is not the same as silence and not the same as added ambience

stages.title: Foley, Sound Effects & Diegesis
stages.description: Most of what you hear in a film was made after the shoot. Foley artists perform it with props, and the designer decides which sounds live inside the story.
learningObjectives: Describe what Foley is and its three main categories
Separate diegetic from non-diegetic sound
Explain why a prop often sounds more real than the real object
Use a library sound under the right Creative Commons licence

explainBack.question: A scene shows a character walking through snow while music plays. Explain which sounds would be Foley, which are diegetic and which are not, and how you could legally use a downloaded snow sound in your edit.
rubric: Foley is everyday sound performed and recorded in post-production to match the picture
Foley is usually split into feet, moves (cloth and body), and specifics (props)
Props are chosen for how they sound, not how they look; for example, cornstarch can stand in for snow
Diegetic sound comes from inside the story world and characters could hear it, even if it is off screen
Non-diegetic sound, such as the score, is heard only by the audience
A Freesound clip is usable under its licence: CC0 needs no credit, CC BY needs credit, and NC forbids commercial use

resources.title: Foley (filmmaking)
resources.description: Where Foley comes from, how it is split up, and the props artists use.
keyPoints: Foley is the reproduction of everyday sound effects added to film and video in post-production
It is named after Jack Foley, a sound-effects artist at Universal
Foley work is usually divided into feet, moves, and specifics
Foley replaces sound that was not captured well on set, or that was covered by unwanted noise
Artists use props that sound right rather than look right, such as cornstarch for snow or coconut halves for hooves

resources.title: What is Diegetic Sound
resources.description: The difference between sound inside the story and sound only the audience hears.
keyPoints: Diegetic sound originates inside the world of the film, so characters could hear it
Dialogue, source music such as a car radio, and sound effects from on-screen action are diegetic
Diegetic sound can be off screen and still belong to the story world
Non-diegetic sound, such as the score or a narrator, is meant only for the audience
Moving a sound between diegetic and non-diegetic is a deliberate storytelling choice

resources.title: The Magic of Making Sound
resources.description: Foley artists at Warner Bros. recreate film sounds with everyday props.
keyPoints: Foley artists perform sounds in sync with the picture on a Foley stage
Everyday objects are used to stand in for what the picture shows
A Foley mixer records and balances the performance
Much of the sound audiences accept as real was made after the shoot

resources.title: Frequently Asked Questions
resources.description: How Freesound's Creative Commons licences work and how to credit a sound.
keyPoints: Each sound on Freesound carries its own licence: CC0, Attribution (CC BY), or Attribution NonCommercial (CC BY-NC)
CC0 lets you use the sound for almost anything, but you cannot claim you made it
Attribution licences require you to credit the author
NonCommercial licences forbid using the sound to make money
A credit names the sound, the user, a link, and the licence

stages.title: Editing & Cleanup
stages.description: Clean steady noise with a noise profile, and do it gently. Heavy reduction leaves artifacts that sound worse than the hiss.
learningObjectives: Pick which kinds of noise noise reduction can remove
Take a noise profile from a noise-only section
Set reduction, sensitivity, and smoothing and listen for artifacts
Order cleanup steps in an edit

explainBack.question: Your dialogue recording has a constant fan hum and one passing car. Explain what noise reduction can and cannot fix here, the two steps to apply it, how you would check you have not overdone it, and what you would do before and after it.
rubric: Noise reduction is meant for constant background noise such as hum, hiss, or a fan, not for one-off sounds like a passing car
Step one is Get Noise Profile from a section that contains only the noise
Step two is selecting the audio and applying the reduction
Start with moderate settings, such as the default 6 dB, and listen to the Residue to hear what is being removed
Too much reduction causes artifacts such as watery musical noise
Clicks or a narrow hum may be better handled with click removal or a notch filter first, and compression comes after cleanup

resources.title: Noise Reduction
resources.description: The two-step noise profile method, what each setting does, and its limits.
keyPoints: Noise Reduction works on constant background noise such as hum, hiss, whine, or fan noise, not on clicks or traffic
Step 1 is Get Noise Profile from a region that contains only noise, at least 2048 samples long
Step 2 is selecting the audio and applying the effect with Noise Reduction (dB), Sensitivity, and Frequency Smoothing
The Residue option lets you hear what is being removed
Too much reduction produces artifacts, including musical noise
Notch filtering or click removal can go before it, and compression after it

resources.title: 🔊 How to use Audacity to Record & Edit Audio | Beginners Tutorial
resources.description: A beginner walkthrough of recording, cleaning, and polishing a voice in Audacity.
keyPoints: Record a few seconds of room noise so you have a clean noise profile
Use Get Noise Profile and then Noise Reduction on the recording
Trim and fade clips so cuts do not click
Apply a compressor to even out the voice after cleanup

stages.title: EQ, Dynamics & Space
stages.description: EQ shapes which frequencies come through, a compressor controls how far the level swings, and reverb places a sound in a room.
learningObjectives: Boost and cut frequency bands with an EQ curve
Explain threshold, ratio, attack, release, and make-up gain
Shape reverb with room size, pre-delay, reverberance, and wet/dry
Avoid clipping while processing

explainBack.question: A voice-over sounds thin, jumps between whispering and shouting, and feels too dry next to a scene recorded in a hall. Explain how you would use EQ, a compressor, and reverb to fix each problem, with the settings that matter.
rubric: EQ boosts or cuts frequency ranges, and cutting low rumble or harsh highs is often cleaner than boosting
Normalize or leave headroom before boosting so the EQ does not clip
A compressor reduces dynamic range: above the threshold, the ratio sets how much the level is turned down
Attack and release set how quickly the compressor reacts and lets go, and make-up gain restores the level afterwards
Reverb room size, pre-delay, and reverberance set the size of the space and how long the tail lasts
Wet and dry levels set how much of the effect is mixed with the original, so the voice can match the hall without washing out

resources.title: Filter Curve EQ
resources.description: Drawing an EQ curve to boost or cut frequencies, with a worked radio example.
keyPoints: An equalizer boosts or cuts chosen frequency ranges
The curve is usually viewed on a logarithmic frequency scale, matching how we hear pitch
A worked example imitates AM radio by cutting below about 100 Hz and above about 6,000 Hz
Normalizing to around -3 dB first leaves headroom so a boost does not clip

resources.title: Compressor
resources.description: How a compressor reduces dynamic range and what each control changes.
keyPoints: A compressor reduces the dynamic range of audio by turning down the loud parts
The threshold is the level above which compression starts, and the ratio sets how strongly it applies
With a -10 dB threshold and a 10:1 ratio, a 0 dB peak comes out at -9 dB
Attack and release times set how fast gain reduction starts and stops; lookahead lets it react before a peak
Make-up gain raises the result back up after compression, and the knee softens the transition at the threshold

resources.title: Reverb
resources.description: The controls that turn a dry recording into one that sounds like it was in a room.
keyPoints: Room Size sets the size of the simulated space
Pre-delay delays the start of the reverb, up to 200 ms
Reverberance sets how long the reverb tail lasts, and Damping softens its high frequencies
Wet Gain and Dry Gain set the balance between the effect and the original
Add silence at the end of a clip so the tail is not cut off

stages.title: Synthesis for Sound Design
stages.description: Many designed sounds start in a synthesizer: a rich oscillator, a filter that carves it, and envelopes that shape it over time.
learningObjectives: Describe the four stages of an ADSR envelope
Explain subtractive synthesis from oscillator to filter
Apply an envelope to amplitude, filter, or pitch
Build a sound by ear in a synth playground

explainBack.question: You need a short plucked sound and a slow swelling pad from the same synthesizer. Explain how subtractive synthesis builds a sound, and how you would set the envelope for each of the two sounds.
rubric: Subtractive synthesis starts with a harmonically rich oscillator, such as a sawtooth or square wave, or noise
A filter, often low-pass, removes overtones to shape the tone
An envelope changes a parameter over time, such as amplitude, filter cutoff, or pitch
Attack is the time to reach peak, decay the time to fall to the sustain level, sustain the level held while the key is down, and release the time to fade after it is let go
A pluck uses a fast attack, short decay, and low sustain; a pad uses a slow attack and a long release

resources.title: Envelope (music)
resources.description: The ADSR envelope and what it controls in a sound.
keyPoints: An envelope describes how a sound changes over time
Attack is the time from nothing to the peak level
Decay is the time from the peak down to the sustain level
Sustain is a level held until the key is released, and release is the time back to nothing
Robert Moog's envelope generator in the 1960s made this control standard; envelopes can drive amplitude, filter cutoff, or pitch

resources.title: Subtractive synthesis
resources.description: How filtering a rich source produces a new timbre.
keyPoints: Subtractive synthesis attenuates the overtones of a harmonically rich source with a filter
Typical sources are sawtooth or square-like waves and noise
A common signal path is oscillator, then filter, then an amplifier shaped by an envelope
A plucked string can be imitated by quickly closing a low-pass filter
It was the dominant method on analog synthesizers

resources.title: Learning Synths
resources.description: An interactive browser playground for oscillators, filters, envelopes, and LFOs.
keyPoints: Runs in the browser with no download
Lessons introduce oscillators, filters, envelopes, and LFOs one at a time
Every control can be heard immediately, so you learn by ear
A free playground lets you build and change a sound yourself

stages.title: Mixing, Loudness & Interactive Audio
stages.description: Finished sound meets a loudness target for where it will play. In games it has to react to the player, so the mix is built to change.
learningObjectives: Explain LUFS loudness targets for broadcast and streaming
Separate integrated loudness from true peak
Describe how a game engine places and mixes sound
Explain why game audio has to be adaptive

explainBack.question: The same sound design has to ship as a broadcast trailer, a Spotify release, and the audio for a small game. Explain the loudness targets you would aim for, why a game needs a different approach, and which tools help with it.
rubric: Loudness is measured in LUFS; EBU R 128 sets a programme loudness target of -23 LUFS for broadcast
Spotify normalizes playback to about -14 LUFS, so a louder master is turned down
True peak should stay below about -1 dBTP to avoid distortion after encoding
Game events happen in an unpredictable order, so the sound has to be dynamic and adaptive
In Unity an Audio Source plays sound and an Audio Listener, usually on the camera, hears it in 3D space
Middleware such as FMOD Studio lets a designer build adaptive events and mix while the game runs

resources.title: R 128 - Loudness normalisation and permitted maximum level of audio signals
resources.description: The broadcast loudness recommendation used across Europe.
keyPoints: EBU R 128 sets a programme loudness target of -23 LUFS
It measures loudness over the whole programme rather than by peak level
It adds Loudness Range and Maximum True Peak Level as descriptors
A small tolerance around the target is allowed
The recommendation has been revised several times, most recently as version 5.0

resources.title: Loudness normalization
resources.description: How Spotify adjusts playback loudness and how to master for it.
keyPoints: Spotify normalizes playback to -14 dB LUFS by default, measured with ITU 1770
Premium listeners can pick Loud (-11), Normal (-14), or Quiet (-19)
A louder master is turned down, so extra loudness gains nothing
Master at about -14 LUFS integrated with true peak below -1 dBTP, or below -2 dBTP for louder masters
Albums are normalized as a whole so the relative levels of tracks stay the same

resources.title: Audio overview
resources.description: How Unity plays, positions, and mixes sound in a 3D scene.
keyPoints: An Audio Source plays a clip from a GameObject, and an Audio Listener, usually on the camera, hears it
Unity simulates distance, position, and the Doppler effect for 3D sound
Reverb Zones and filters such as Echo add environmental effects
The Audio Mixer groups and balances sources
Unity imports AIFF, WAV, MP3, and Ogg files

resources.title: Welcome to FMOD Studio
resources.description: The adaptive audio tool designers use to build game sound without programming.
keyPoints: FMOD Studio is built for creating adaptive audio for games
Its interface is similar to a DAW, so sound designers can work without writing code
Events react to what happens in the game
Designers can mix and adjust audio live while the game runs, and profile it

resources.title: Sound design
resources.description: Sound design across film, television, theatre, and games.
keyPoints: Sound design is used in film, television, theatre, music, and video games
Walter Murch was the first person credited as Sound Designer, in 1969
Game sound has to be dynamic and adaptive because events happen in an unpredictable order
Theatre sound designers place cues in the show and often run them with software such as QLab

name: Sound Design
description: Learn how to hear, record, and build sound for a scene: the physics of sound, digital audio, microphones and room tone, Foley and diegesis, cleanup, EQ and dynamics, synthesis, and loudness for film, streaming, and games.
